E0A01: A ground rod's job is lightning: it gives a strike a path into the earth. Keeping RF off the cables between pieces of gear is bonding, a separate job.
E0A02: Neighbors are the general public, so the uncontrolled limits apply (they don't know they're being exposed). MPE stands for maximum permissible Exposure, not emission.
E0A03: 30-300 MHz (VHF) is where the human body resonates: a body is roughly a half wavelength long there. That's why the limits are tightest in that range.
E0A04: Multi-transmitter site: anyone producing 5% or more of their own MPE limit shares responsibility. Memory hook: five percent, you're in.
E0A05: Microwaves aren't ionizing. The danger is concentration: high-gain dishes focus the energy into a tight, intense beam.
E0A06: All three are true. The body reacts to both fields, the fields vary with location, and their peaks don't line up. Below 300 MHz you're often in the near field.
E0A07: 100% tie-off means you're always connected: at least one lanyard is attached at every moment, even while you move.
E0A08: SAR stands for specific absorption rate: how fast the body absorbs RF energy, measured in watts per kilogram.
E0A09: The only exemption left: handhelds sold before May 3, 2021 (grandfathered when the rules changed). There's no low-power exemption anymore.
E0A10: The old exemptions based on power or mode are gone. An evaluation must always be performed.
E0A11: Clip lanyards to the tower legs, the strongest structural members. Not the rungs, the mast, or the guy brackets.
E0A12: Attach the shock-absorbing lanyard above your head, so a fall is short and the lanyard catches you sooner.
E1A01: USB spreads upward from the carrier. 14.348 + 3 kHz = 14.351 MHz, but 20 m ends at 14.350. The top 1 kHz is out of band.
E1A02: LSB spreads downward from the carrier. A 3 kHz-wide LSB signal needs the carrier at least 3 kHz above the lower band edge.
E1A03: The 20 m data segment ends at 14.150 MHz. USB spreads upward, so the highest carrier is 14.150 - 0.0028 = 14.1472 MHz.
E1A04: Extra-class 75 m phone starts at 3.600 MHz. LSB on 3.601 spreads about 3 kHz down to around 3.598, below the phone edge.
E1A05: On a US-registered vessel, any FCC amateur licensee (or an authorized reciprocal operator) can be the control operator. No marine license is needed.
E1A06: 60 m channels: CW goes at the channel's center frequency. (For USB, the carrier sits 1.5 kHz below center.)
E1A07: 2200 m: 1 watt EIRP. Memory hook: the bigger band number (2200) gets the smaller power (1 W). 630 m gets 5 W.
E1A08: In message forwarding, the originating station's control operator is primarily accountable: whoever put the message on the air first.
E1A09: 630 m: 5 watts EIRP. Memory hook: the smaller band number (630) gets the bigger power (5 W). 2200 m gets 1 W.
E1A10: Aboard a ship or aircraft, the master of the ship or pilot in command must approve. The captain rules.
E1A11: Any FCC-issued amateur license works aboard a US-registered vessel, even in international waters. No special endorsement is needed.
E1B01: Spurious emission: energy outside the necessary bandwidth that can be removed without losing any information (harmonics, parasitics).
E1B02: Digital voice or SSTV on HF: 3 kHz, the same width as an SSB voice signal.
E1B03: Protect an FCC monitoring facility within 1 mile.
E1B04: Radiolocation is primary on 70 cm and hams are secondary. If your repeater interferes with it, you stop or fix it.
E1B05: The National Radio Quiet Zone surrounds the National Radio Astronomy Observatory at Green Bank, West Virginia.
E1B06: Near an airport, you may have to notify the FAA and register the tower with the FCC under Part 17. Memory hook: Part 17 = towers.
E1B07: PRB-1 covers state and local zoning. It doesn't cover HOAs, whose rules are private covenants.
E1B08: If you interfere with well-designed broadcast receivers, the FCC can impose quiet hours on the offending frequencies. Not a full shutdown.
E1B09: RACES: any FCC-licensed amateur station that the local civil defense organization certifies.
E1B10: Under RACES you use every frequency the control operator's license allows. No special channels.
E1B11: PRB-1 requires reasonable accommodation of amateur antennas, not unlimited antennas.
E1C01: 60 m data: 2.8 kHz maximum bandwidth, the same as the 60 m channel width for USB.
E1C02: With foreign stations: only communications incidental to the amateur service, plus remarks of a personal nature.
E1C03: After notifying the UTC about 630 or 2200 m: wait 30 days. If they haven't said you're within 1 km of power-line carrier (PLC) systems, you can operate.
E1C04: IARP stands for International Amateur Radio Permit, for certain countries in the Americas. Memory hook: IARP = Americas, CEPT = Europe.
E1C05: Third-party traffic under automatic control: only RTTY or data emissions.
E1C06: Operating under CEPT: carry a copy of FCC Public Notice DA 16-1048. (Your call sign takes the host country's prefix, not /CEPT.)
E1C07: Before using 630 or 2200 m, tell the Utilities Technology Council (UTC) your call sign and station coordinates. Power companies use those frequencies for PLC.
E1C08: If a remote-control link fails, the station must stop transmitting within 3 minutes.
E1C09: FM or PM below 29 MHz: the maximum modulation index is 1.0 at the highest modulation frequency. That keeps HF FM narrow.
E1C10: Spurious emissions below 30 MHz: at least 43 dB below the fundamental (-43 dB).
E1C11: CEPT = Europe (two-way: US hams there, European hams here). IARP = the Americas.
E1C12: 630 m allows phone across the entire band (472-479 kHz).
E1D01: Telemetry = one-way measurements sent from a distance. Memory hook: tele-METRY, METeR readings. Telecommand is the one that controls a device.
E1D02: Encryption is allowed only for telecommand of a space station, so nobody can hijack a satellite.
E1D03: A space telecommand station sends commands up to a satellite: it initiates, modifies, or terminates the satellite's functions.
E1D04: A balloon telemetry station identifies with just its call sign.
E1D05: A station operated by telecommand on or near Earth must post all of these: a copy of the license, plus labels with the licensee's and the control operator's contact info.
E1D06: Model craft by telecommand: 1 watt maximum.
E1D07: HF space stations: 40, 20, 15, and 10 m. Pick the answer without 30 m, which has no space-station allocation.
E1D08: VHF space stations: 2 m only. Not 6 m, not 1.25 m.
E1D09: UHF space stations: 70 cm and 13 cm. Not 33 cm.
E1D10: A space station's telecommand stations are whichever stations the space station licensee designates.
E1D11: Earth stations: any amateur station, within the control operator's privileges. Even a Technician can work satellites.
E1D12: One-way transmissions are allowed for space stations, beacons, and telecommand stations. Repeaters and forwarding systems are two-way.
E1E01: VEs and VECs can be reimbursed only for exam costs: preparing, processing, administering, and coordinating. Not for teaching or study materials.
E1E02: The VECs maintain the question pools (through the NCVEC Question Pool Committee).
E1E03: A VEC is an organization with an FCC agreement to coordinate exams. A VE is a person.
E1E04: VE accreditation comes from a VEC, which confirms you meet the FCC requirements. It isn't automatic and it doesn't come from the FCC.
E1E05: If the examinee fails, hand the application back to them.
E1E06: Every administering VE is responsible for the session's conduct, not just the session manager.
E1E07: If a candidate ignores the examiner's instructions, terminate that candidate's exam immediately. No warning, and only theirs.
E1E08: A VE may not examine relatives listed in the FCC rules. Friends and employees are allowed.
E1E09: A fraudulent VE has their station license revoked and their operator license suspended.
E1E10: After a pass, the VEs submit the application to the coordinating VEC, following the VEC's instructions. The VEC forwards it to the FCC.
E1E11: After a pass, three VEs must certify the examinee is qualified and that they followed the rules. When in doubt on VE questions, think three VEs.
E1F01: Spread spectrum is allowed only above 222 MHz. Memory hook: SS starts at 222.
E1F02: A Canadian license in the US: the Canadian license's privileges, capped at US Amateur Extra.
E1F03: An uncertified amplifier for below 144 MHz can only be sold if a ham built or modified it for amateur use.
E1F04: Line A runs roughly parallel to and just south of the US-Canada border.
E1F05: North of Line A: no transmitting on 420-430 MHz, which Canada uses. Memory hook: Line A blocks 420-430.
E1F06: The FCC issues a Special Temporary Authority (STA) for experimental amateur communications.
E1F07: You can send a message to a business only if neither you nor your employer has a pecuniary (money) interest in it.
E1F08: Prohibited: communications for hire or compensation. Politics, religion, and other languages are all allowed.
E1F09: Mesh networks can't carry messages encoded to obscure their meaning (no encryption). Email and third-party traffic are fine.
E1F10: Auxiliary station control operator: Technician or higher, so any current license class.
E1F11: Amplifier certification: it must meet the spurious emission standards at the lesser of 1500 W or its full output.
E2A01: Ascending pass = the satellite is climbing northward: it travels from south to north. Descending is north to south.
E2A02: All three are true of an inverting transponder: sidebands swap, positions in the band flip, and the uplink and downlink Doppler shifts partly cancel.
E2A03: An inverting transponder mixes the uplink with a local oscillator and transmits the difference product. Taking the difference is what flips the spectrum.
E2A04: A satellite's mode = its uplink and downlink bands, for example mode U/V (UHF up, VHF down).
E2A05: Mode letters name the uplink and downlink frequency ranges (V = 2 m, U = 70 cm, L = 23 cm, S = 13 cm).
E2A06: Keplerian elements (named for Kepler, who worked out orbits) are the numbers that define a satellite's orbit. Tracking software uses them.
E2A07: A linear transponder relays whatever you send it, so all of these work: FM, CW, SSB, SSTV, PSK, packet.
E2A08: Users of a linear transponder share its downlink power. One loud uplink hogs it and weakens everyone else, so keep your ERP reasonable.
E2A09: L band = 23 cm (1.2 GHz). S band = 13 cm (2.4 GHz). Alphabetical order matches: L is lower than S.
E2A10: Geostationary: the satellite orbits at the same rate Earth turns, so it appears fixed in the sky.
E2A11: A circularly polarized antenna doesn't care which way the signal's polarization is rotated, so it beats spin modulation and Faraday rotation.
E2A12: Store-and-forward: the satellite holds messages and downloads them later, when it passes over the receiving station.
E2B01: A coding rate of 3/4 means 3 of every 4 bits are data and 1 in 4 (25%) is forward error correction.
E2B02: An NTSC frame has 525 lines. Memory hook: 525 is the classic US TV number.
E2B03: Interlaced: odd-numbered lines in one field, even-numbered lines in the next. Two fields make one frame.
E2B04: Analog SSTV sends color one color line at a time, sequentially (for example red, then green, then blue).
E2B05: Vestigial sideband trims most of one sideband to save bandwidth, while keeping the low-frequency video components accurate.
E2B06: Vestigial sideband = AM sending one complete sideband plus a vestige (a leftover portion) of the other.
E2B07: DVB-T, digital TV, uses QAM and QPSK. Digital TV packs bits into phase and amplitude.
E2B08: 70 cm ATV fits into the cable TV channels, so a cable-ready analog TV can tune it.
E2B09: DRM digital SSTV is decoded with an SSB receiver plus software. It fits in a voice-width channel.
E2B10: In analog SSTV, brightness is the tone frequency: lower pitch is darker, higher is brighter.
E2B11: The VIS code at the start of an SSTV transmission tells the receiving software which SSTV mode is being sent.
E2B12: SSTV sync is a specific tone frequency (1200 Hz) that tells the software to start a new line.
E2C01: Operating remotely with the transmitter inside the US needs no extra indicator. Just use your normal call sign.
E2C02: ADIF (Amateur Data Interchange Format) is the format for moving logs between programs. Compare Cabrillo, which is for contest log submission.
E2C03: No contesting on 30 m. It's a WARC band, and the WARC bands (30, 17, 12 m) are kept contest-free.
E2C04: Mesh networks use frequencies shared with unlicensed Wi-Fi services. They run on Wi-Fi gear (see E2C09).
E2C05: A DX QSL manager handles a DX station's QSL cards and confirmations.
E2C06: In VHF/UHF contests, SSB and CW activity sits in the weak-signal segment, clustered near the calling frequency.
E2C07: Cabrillo is the standard format for submitting contest logs. ADIF is for general log exchange.
E2C08: LoTW can confirm all of these: US special events, US-to-DX contacts, and Worked All States.
E2C09: An amateur mesh network is built from wireless routers running custom firmware (AREDN, for example).
E2C10: All three reasons: the DX frequency may be off-limits to some callers, splitting separates the callers from the DX, and it's more efficient.
E2C11: In a pileup, send your full call sign once or twice. Never partial calls, never the long-winded version.
E2C12: Latency = the delay between an action and its result. It matters in remote operation.
E2D01: MSK144 is the meteor scatter mode: fast, to catch short pings off meteor trails.
E2D02: FT8 or FT4 in a VHF contest: the exchange uses your grid square in place of the signal report.
E2D03: Q65 is designed for EME (moonbounce). Memory hook: Q65 for the Moon, MSK144 for meteors.
E2D04: Amateur balloons are tracked in real time with APRS position reports.
E2D05: JT65 decodes signals far below the noise, at very low signal-to-noise ratios. The 65 is its 65 tones, not its bandwidth or baud rate.
E2D06: EME contacts use timed, synchronized transmissions: stations take turns in fixed periods.
E2D07: APRS rides on AX.25 packet radio.
E2D08: APRS beacons are unnumbered information (UI) frames: broadcast with no connection or acknowledgment.
E2D09: JT65 is multitone AFSK: 65 audio tones.
E2D10: WIDE3-1: 3 digipeater hops were requested and 1 hop remains. The second number counts down.
E2D11: APRS data is relayed by packet digipeaters.
E2E01: HF data (below 30 MHz) uses FSK, as in RTTY and many digital modes.
E2E02: WSJT-X modes (FT8 and others) depend on accurate computer clocks. If your clock is off, you won't decode.
E2E03: FT4: the 4 = four-tone continuous-phase FSK. FT8 uses 8 tones.
E2E04: All of these describe FST4: 4-tone Gaussian FSK, variable transmit/receive periods, and several tone spacings.
E2E05: WSPR is beacon-only (propagation reports), so it doesn't support keyboard-to-keyboard chat.
E2E06: An FT8 transmission cycle is 15 seconds.
E2E07: Q65 averages multiple receive cycles to pull out very weak signals. That's its edge over JT65.
E2E08: PACTOR (an ARQ mode) can transfer binary files error-free.
E2E09: PSK31 uses varicode, a variable-length character code: common letters get shorter codes, like Morse.
E2E10: FT8 is about 50 Hz wide, narrower than RTTY, MFSK16, or PACTOR IV.
E2E11: Direct FSK shifts the transmitter's VFO itself. Audio FSK feeds shifting audio tones into SSB.
E2E12: ALE radios keep scanning a list of frequencies and come alive when they hear their own call sign.
E2E13: PACTOR IV has the highest throughput, the fastest of the choices in good conditions.
E3A01: EME range: about 12,000 miles, half the Earth's circumference, as long as both stations can see the Moon.
E3A02: Libration fading: a fluttery, irregular fading caused by the Moon's slight wobble.
E3A03: Least EME path loss at perigee, when the Moon is closest to Earth.
E3A04: An electromagnetic wave travels at right angles to both its electric and its magnetic field.
E3A05: The E and H fields in a wave are at right angles to each other (perpendicular).
E3A06: When the MUF drops (at night), switch to a lower frequency band.
E3A07: Microwave ducts often form over large bodies of water, where temperature inversions are common.
E3A08: Meteor trails ionize the E region, about 100 km up.
E3A09: Meteor scatter works best from 28 to 148 MHz (10 m to 2 m), with 6 m the classic band.
E3A10: A wave's speed in a medium is set by the medium's index of refraction.
E3A11: Tropospheric ducting of microwaves: typically 100 to 300 miles.
E3A12: Aurora comes from severe geomagnetic storms.
E3A13: CW is best for aurora. The signal comes back raspy and distorted, and CW survives that best.
E3A14: Circular polarization: the electric and magnetic fields rotate as the wave travels.
E3B01: TEP: points 2,000 to 3,000 miles apart on a path that crosses the geomagnetic equator at right angles (north-south).
E3B02: TEP maximum range is about 5,000 miles.
E3B03: TEP peaks in the afternoon or early evening.
E3B04: Ordinary and extraordinary waves: the ionosphere splits a signal into two independently propagating, elliptically polarized waves.
E3B05: 160 m DX needs a path entirely in darkness, because sunlight's D-layer absorbs low frequencies.
E3B06: Long-path propagation is most common on 40 and 20 m.
E3B07: A lower takeoff (elevation) angle makes each skip hop longer.
E3B08: Ground wave fades faster at higher frequencies, so its range decreases as frequency goes up.
E3B09: Sporadic-E peaks around the solstices, especially the summer solstice (summer Es season).
E3B10: Chordal hop skips the ground bounces, so the signal loses less than in normal multi-hop.
E3B11: Sporadic-E happens mostly during daylight, between sunrise and sunset.
E3B12: Chordal hop: successive refractions inside the ionosphere with no ground reflection in between.
E3B13: Ground wave supports vertical polarization. Horizontal polarization is shorted out by the ground.
E3C01: Short-term radio blackouts come from solar flares (X-rays hit within minutes). CMEs take days to arrive.
E3C02: A rising A-index or K-index means the geomagnetic field is getting more disturbed.
E3C03: When A or K is high, paths through the auroral oval suffer the most absorption.
E3C04: Bz = the north-south component of the interplanetary magnetic field.
E3C05: A southward Bz lets solar particles couple into Earth's field. Memory hook: south = storms.
E3C06: The VHF/UHF radio horizon is about 15% farther than the visual horizon, because the atmosphere bends the signal slightly.
E3C07: Flare classes run A, B, C, M, X, and X is strongest. There's no class Z.
E3C08: Geomagnetic storm scale runs G1 to G5. G5 is extreme.
E3C09: Propagation reporting networks (PSK Reporter, RBN, WSPRnet) report received digital-mode and CW signals.
E3C10: 304A = ultraviolet emissions at 304 angstroms, which track the solar flux index.
E3C12: A sudden rise in noise across HF means a CME impact or solar flare has occurred.
E4A01: A digital scope can only show what it samples. The ADC's sampling rate sets the highest frequency it displays accurately.
E4A02: Spectrum analyzer: vertical axis = amplitude, horizontal axis = frequency. (An oscilloscope is amplitude vs. time.)
E4A03: Spurs and intermod products are extra frequencies, and a spectrum analyzer shows frequencies.
E4A04: Probe compensation: display a square wave and adjust until its flat tops and bottoms are as flat as possible (no overshoot or rounding).
E4A05: A prescaler divides a high frequency down into the counter's range. It divides, never multiplies.
E4A06: Aliasing comes from sampling too slowly. It shows a false, jittery low-frequency version of the waveform.
E4A07: An antenna analyzer computes SWR and impedance for you. It measures; it doesn't tune the antenna.
E4A08: All of these measure SWR: a directional wattmeter, a vector network analyzer, and an antenna analyzer.
E4A09: Keep the probe's ground lead short. A long ground lead adds inductance and causes ringing.
E4A10: Ripple from a linear supply is locked to the AC line, so trigger on Line.
E4A11: An antenna analyzer can measure all of these: velocity factor, cable length, and the resonant frequency of a tuned circuit.
E4B01: A frequency counter is only as accurate as its time base, the reference clock it counts against.
E4B02: Ohms per volt x full-scale volts = the meter's input impedance. Higher means less loading of the circuit.
E4B03: S21 = forward gain (in at port 1, out at port 2). Read it as 'to 2, from 1'.
E4B04: S11 = reflection at the input port (in at 1, back out at 1): return loss, SWR.
E4B05: VNA calibration uses three loads: short, open, and a 50-ohm load (SOL).
E4B07: S-parameter subscripts are port numbers: S21 = out at port 2, from a signal in at port 1.
E4B08: Q = resonant frequency / bandwidth. Measure the bandwidth of the frequency response and you can find Q.
E4B09: A two-port VNA measures transmission through a device, so it can show a filter's frequency response.
E4B10: Two-tone test: feed two non-harmonically related audio (AF) tones into the mic input and look at the RF output on a spectrum analyzer.
E4B11: A VNA can measure all of these: input impedance, output impedance, and reflection coefficient.
E4C01: Phase noise on the master clock mixes with strong nearby signals and creates interference. That's reciprocal mixing (see E4C13).
E4C02: Strong out-of-band signals are stopped at the front door: a front-end filter or preselector.
E4C03: Capture effect: FM locks onto the stronger signal and suppresses the weaker one on the same frequency.
E4C04: Noise figure = how much more noise the receiver makes than a theoretically perfect one, in dB.
E4C05: -174 dBm is the theoretical noise in a 1 Hz bandwidth at room temperature, the floor of a perfect receiver.
E4C08: An SDR overloads when the input exceeds the ADC's reference voltage. Past that, the converter clips.
E4C09: A high IF puts the image frequency far from the wanted one (image = 2 x IF away), so front-end filters can remove it easily.
E4C10: Match the receive bandwidth to the signal: best signal-to-noise, least interference.
E4C11: On low HF bands, atmospheric noise is far above the receiver's own noise, so attenuating cuts signal and noise together. SNR barely changes.
E4C12: A roofing filter is narrow, early in the receiver: it knocks down strong nearby signals, improving blocking dynamic range.
E4C13: Reciprocal mixing: local oscillator phase noise mixes with strong adjacent signals and puts noise on top of the signal you want.
E4C14: IF shift slides the passband to dodge an interfering station on an adjacent frequency.
E4D01: Blocking dynamic range: from the noise floor up to the signal level that causes 1 dB of gain compression.
E4D02: Poor dynamic range shows up as cross-modulation spurs and desensitization from strong nearby signals.
E4D03: Repeater intermod: the two output signals mix in one transmitter's final amplifier.
E4D04: A circulator (properly terminated) on the transmitter output blocks signals coming backward into the final amp, so they can't mix there.
E4D06: Desensitization (desense): a strong nearby signal reduces the receiver's sensitivity.
E4D07: Fix desense with attenuation before the first RF stage. More front-end gain makes it worse.
E4D08: Intermodulation comes from nonlinear circuits or devices. A perfectly linear circuit can't mix.
E4D09: A preselector improves rejection of signals outside the band you're receiving.
E4D10: Third-order intercept (IP3) is a theoretical point: two input signals at that level would make a third-order product as strong as the inputs. Higher is better.
E4D11: Odd-order products (like 2f1 - f2) land close to the original signals, inside the band you're receiving.
E4D14: -100 dBm = 10^-10 mW = 10^-13 W = 0.1 picowatt. Every -30 dBm divides by 1000: -30 dBm = 1 uW, -60 = 1 nW, -90 = 1 pW.
E4E01: An automatic notch hunts for steady carriers, and a CW signal is a steady carrier, so it can notch out the CW too.
E4E02: DSP noise reduction can help with all of these: white noise, ignition noise, and power line noise.
E4E03: A noise blanker removes impulse noise (short, sharp pops like ignition).
E4E04: Alternator and charging noise: ferrite chokes on the charging system leads.
E4E05: AC motor RFI: a brute-force AC-line filter in series with the motor's power leads.
E4E06: Network gear makes unstable carriers, modulated or not, at specific frequencies.
E4E07: Shielded cables radiate when common-mode current flows on the shield and conductors.
E4E08: Common-mode current flows the same way on all conductors at once, as if the cable were one wire.
E4E09: A noise blanker can be fooled by strong signals: they get distorted and look like spurious signals.
E4E10: All of these cause roaring or buzzing AC line noise: arcing thermostats, bad doorbell transformers, faulty lighted signs.
E4E11: Corroded metal joints act like diodes. They mix broadcast signals and reradiate new ones (the rusty bolt effect).
E4E12: Carriers at regular intervals across a wide range = switch-mode power supply harmonics.
E4E13: The surge protector goes on the single point ground panel, so everything shares one ground reference.
E4E14: A single point ground panel makes all the lightning protectors share one ground, so they activate together.
E5A01: At resonance, XL and XC cancel each other overall, but each one still carries the full current, so the voltage across each reactance can be Q times the applied voltage.
E5A02: f = 1 / (2 pi sqrt(LC)). R doesn't change resonance. 1 / (2 pi sqrt(50 uH x 40 pF)) = 3.56 MHz.
E5A03: Series resonance: XL and XC cancel, leaving only R. So impedance is about equal to the circuit resistance (a minimum).
E5A04: Parallel RLC at resonance: the L and C branches cancel each other, leaving only R. Same answer as for series: about equal to the circuit resistance.
E5A05: Higher Q means a sharper, narrower response, so matching bandwidth decreases.
E5A06: Parallel LC at resonance: energy sloshes back and forth between L and C, so the circulating current is at its maximum.
E5A07: Parallel resonance has maximum impedance, so the current drawn at the input is at its minimum.
E5A08: At resonance the reactances cancel, the circuit looks purely resistive, and voltage and current are in phase.
E5A09: Parallel Q = R / X. Series Q is the flip: X / R.
E5A10: f = 1 / (2 pi sqrt(LC)) = 1 / (2 pi sqrt(50 uH x 10 pF)) = 7.12 MHz. R is a decoy.
E5A13: Higher Q in a series resonant circuit means higher internal voltages across L and C (Q times the applied voltage).
E5B01: One time constant (RC) = charging to 63.2%, or discharging to 36.8%.
E5B02: Susceptance = B. (G = conductance, X = reactance, Y = admittance.) Memory hook: suscepta-B-ce.
E5B03: Impedance to admittance in polar form: take 1 / magnitude and flip the sign of the angle.
E5B04: Two 220 uF in parallel = 440 uF. Two 1 Mohm in parallel = 0.5 Mohm. RC = 440 uF x 0.5 Mohm = 220 s.
E5B05: Susceptance is just the reciprocal of reactance: B = 1/X.
E5B06: Susceptance is the imaginary part of admittance (Y = G + jB).
E5B07: Net X = XL - XC = 250 - 500 = -250 (capacitive). Angle = arctan(250/1000) = 14 deg. Capacitive means voltage lags current.
E5B08: Net X = 100 - 300 = -200 (capacitive). Angle = arctan(200/100) = 63 deg. Capacitive means voltage lags current.
E5B09: Capacitor: current leads voltage by 90 deg. Memory hook: ELI the ICE man: in a C, I comes before E.
E5B10: Inductor: voltage leads current by 90 deg. Memory hook: ELI the ICE man: in an L, E comes before I.
E5B11: Net X = 75 - 25 = +50 (inductive). Angle = arctan(50/100) = 27 deg. Inductive means voltage leads current.
E5B12: Admittance is the inverse of impedance: Y = 1/Z.
E5C01: Capacitive reactance is negative j: pure 100 ohms capacitive = 0 - j100.
E5C02: Polar form = magnitude and phase angle. Rectangular form = real and imaginary (R and X).
E5C03: Pure inductive reactance points straight up: +90 deg. Capacitive is -90 deg.
E5C04: Frequency response graphs usually use a logarithmic scale (dB).
E5C05: A phasor diagram shows the phase relationships between impedances at one frequency.
E5C06: 50 - j25: 50 ohms resistance, and the minus j means 25 ohms of capacitive reactance.
E5C07: Pure resistance has no reactance, so it sits on the horizontal (R) axis.
E5C08: Phase angles are shown in polar coordinates (magnitude and angle).
E5C09: Rectangular impedance plot: X axis = resistance, Y axis = reactance (+ inductive, - capacitive).
E5C10: XC = 1 / (2 pi x 14 MHz x 38 pF), about 300 ohms. So 400 - j300: right 400, down 300, which is point 4.

E9H06: Tune a Beverage's termination resistor for the least SWR variation across the band.
E9H07: The Beverage termination resistor absorbs signals arriving from the reverse direction.
E9H08: A sense antenna turns a loop's two nulls into a single null, resolving the 180-degree ambiguity.
E9H09: A terminated single-turn loop (pennant) has a cardioid pattern.
E9H10: More turns and/or more loop area means more output voltage.
E9H11: A cardioid has a single null, which points to the transmitter unambiguously.
